articleTitle: Untangling the Dark Web: Taking on the Human Sex Trafficking Industry
abstract: In 2010, Rane Johnson-Stempson, principal research director at Microsoft Research Connections, formed a partnership with Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) and danah boyd, a senior researcher at Microsoft Research New England, to initiate a research collaborative into the online sex trafficking of minors.

articleTitle: Studying Stereotypes: Examining Why Many Women Do Not Pursue STEM Careers [The Good, the Bad, & the Ugly: Engineering FACTS]
abstract: Dr. Sapna Cheryan, assistant professor at the University of Washington, has spent the last 12 years researching cultural and gender stereotypes, paying particular attention to the reasons many women do not pursue careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields, such as computer science. Here she explains why she started researching this area, how these stereotypes are perpetuated, and what can be done to help future generations of women battle any preconceived notions that might keep them from pursuing their desired paths.

articleTitle: A Biomedical Engineering Story: Rutherford Inspires Young Adults [Women to Watch]
abstract: A biomedical engineer, Kathleen Rutherford is associate director of regulatory affairs at Zimmer Trabecular Metal Technology.

articleTitle: An Energetic Career: Ross Points to the Power of Teamwork [Women to Watch]
abstract: Mari-Louise Ross is no ordinary engineer. Born and raised in South Africa, she just celebrated her four-year anniversary in the United States. Ross says that she's excited about the opportunities to learn and grow as a professional here in America. "This is truly a privilege and I want to make good use of that."

articleTitle: IEEE WIE Charter on ?The Hill? at AAMU: Collaboration Seeks Diversity [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: IEEE Women in Engineering (WIE) has extended its hand to reach out to groups that are below the radar for a long time?groups that are intellectual, diverse, dynamic, creative, and persevering yet often quietly present in a field that is just as diverse and dynamic as the groups that struggle to maintain their presence and be heard?groups such as the female engineering and computer science undergraduate students at Alabama A&M University (AAMU) on ?The Hill? in Huntsville, Alabama. WIE set its sights to collaborate with the group at AAMU as part of promoting and seeking out the diverse talents of more underrepresented groups in the area. Although the female students that represent electrical engineering and computer science are small in number at AAMU, their interests, ideals, and voice to promote the engineering program at AAMU as they aspire to join the global world of engineering is bold, vibrant, and substantient.

articleTitle: Folding Matters: Compacting Big Ideas [Lesson Plan]
abstract: Did you know that origami and engineering share something in common? Folding! From heart stents, to airbags, to collapsible solar panels on spacecraft, folding lets engineers fit big ideas into small packages.

articleTitle: Making It All Compute: Busting Cultural Barriers from Egypt to the United States
abstract: Lamia Youseff, a project manager at Google, was a few years into her graduate program in computer science at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), when she suddenly noticed that she was the only female student in her advanced operating systems class. She was somewhat baffled. Her undergraduate class in computer science at The American University in Cairo had been 50% men and 50% women, and it was common for a female student to be at the top of the class. "I never realized that computer science as a field is a male-dominated field until I moved to the U.S.," she says. "Luckily," she adds, "I was the top student in that class as well."

articleTitle: Talking SSIT: Society President Jacob Focuses on Engagement [Women to Watch]
abstract: Laura Jacob, president of the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology (SSIT), first became interested in engineering when she was a young girl. "I was always interested in how things work," she says. Savvy with technology, Jacob says she always knew she could excel at it and thought it would be a great career field to pursue. She went to the University of Connecticut and transferred to Pace University, where she earned a bachelor's degree in computer science. After college, Jacob explains that she stayed involved in IEEE, partly because her professors encouraged her to do so. "Being involved in the IEEE has been very good for my career, it's a great place to meet other professionals and share ideas," she adds.

IEEE Keywords: IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology

articleTitle: A President of Relevance: Novak to Assume IPS President Role [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Next year when Dalma Novak takes over as president of the IEEE Photonics Society (IPS), she'll have one main goal in mind: relevance. "I've been thinking about that a lot over the last few months," she says, referring to her vision for the Society. "I want to understand what the Society should be doing to keep itself relevant and how it can change as the needs of its members and stakeholders change."

articleTitle: Finding Common Ground : Focusing on Workplace Transition [Career Advisor]
abstract: The transition from college to professional work can be difficult for most new college graduates. Kim Conrad and Marissa Carrillo initially embarked on different career paths, but each eventually found a common interest in civil engineering. Their respective journeys have intersected, resulting in an unexpected work dynamic. Both are currently project engineers at Crowley Engineering LLC, a niche consulting engineering firm, solving major infrastructure challenges for industrial and commercial clients.

articleTitle: Future Cities Ideas are "Sim"ering: Marinovici Serves as Middle School Mentor [Pipelining: Attractive Programs for Women]
abstract: The kids in Pasco, Washington, may not have exposure to the big city, but that didn't stop them from participating in the 2013 Future Cities Challenge. Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) Software Engineer Cristina Marinovici mentored a team of middle school students from the Ellen Ochoa Middle School as they imagined, designed, and built cities of the future.

articleTitle: Keeping an Open Mind: Brooks Finds Rewards in Volunteering [Women to Watch]
abstract: When Kristi Brooks quit her job to stay at home with her small children, she thought not having a full-time job meant some free time to volunteer with IEEE. Little did she know that what started out as a way to reconnect with a group she had belonged to as a student would turn into a full-fledged love of over 15 years, remaining strong even after she returned to a challenging role as a design engineer.

articleTitle: Making Connections: Barth Among Women Thriving at GSFC [Women to Watch]
abstract: When Janet Barth was selected to be chief of the Electrical Engineering Division (EED) at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC), it shouldn't have been all that surprising. Nobody could dispute that she was highly experienced. Over the years, she had risen through the ranks at the GSFC, from a co-op student in 1976 to manager of the Flight Data Systems and Radiation Effects Branch of the EED from 2005 to 2008. But there were a couple of distinctions. For one thing, she had never been an associate division chief. And, unlike all of the other division heads, she was a woman. "I'm so fortunate that the other division chiefs - all men, of course - were very helpful," she says. "I could always call them to ask for advice."

articleTitle: The Power of PRASAD: Working for Sustainable Change
abstract: Even before Dr. M. Cecilia Escarra became the executive director of the PRASAD Project, her values were closely aligned with its mission. PRASAD, a not-for-profit organization, is ?committed to improving the quality of life of economically disadvantaged people around the world,? according to its Web site. Escarra explains that the organization chooses its projects by going to communities and asking the residents how PRASAD can help them overcome their most pressing challenges.

articleTitle: Intellectual Property: The Intersection of Law and Innovation: An Interview with Maura Moran [The Good, the Bad, & the Ugly: Engineering FACTS]
abstract: Maura Moran likes to tell her kids that we don't find our careers, our careers find us. "It's the opportunities that are thrown at us and it's whether we choose to take them - that's what marks our path," she says.

articleTitle: Silicon Valley Star: Stelar-Migotti Has Become a "Hero in Tech"
abstract: There's a well-known expression that you should "reach for the moon, even if you miss, you'll land among the stars." As a young girl hoping to become an astronomer, Maya Strelar-Migotti once reached for the stars - but landed in Silicon Valley. Currently the vice president of IP and Broadband Development at Ericsson, Strelar-Migotti settled in California's Silicon Valley in 2009, residing in five different countries (one of them twice) along the way.

articleTitle: Waging a Battle for Gender Equity: Swiss Advocates Balancing Male and Female Strengths
abstract: In the United States today, there is still a gender pay gap. The National Committee on Pay Equity reports that women working full time earn 77% on the male dollar, and, according to The WAGE Project, a nonprofit organization dedicated to ending workplace discrimination against women, during "her working life, a woman will earn US$1 million less than a man simply because she is a woman." No doubt, the gap has narrowed slightly over the past few decades. In 1980, American women made about 64% as much as men. Yet the wage gap remains one indication that gender inequity in the workplace persists.

articleTitle: America's Top Young Scientist: Kurup Scores Top Prize [Pipelining: Attractive Programs for Women]
abstract: Ninth grader Deepika Kurup is the winner of the 2012 Discovery Education 3M Young Scientist Challenge, which earned her the title ?America?s Top Young Scientist? and an award of US$25,000 for her work. Since 2008, Discovery Education and 3M have held an annual competition encouraging young innovators to develop solutions to everyday problems, competing for a title and cash prizes. At the final competition, the finalists shared their completed innovations with a panel of judges. In addition to presenting their prototypes, the ten finalists competed in two additional challenges in which they were asked to combine multiple 3M technologies to yield new solutions and to build a machine designed to turn on a light bulb using science and engineering principles. Finalists were evaluated on their scientific knowledge, creativity and use of 3M technology.

articleTitle: Under Pressure: Engineering Is a Part of Life for Kotb [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Madiha Kotb is head of the Pressure Vessels Technical Services Division for Regie du batiment du Qu?bec, a board established by the Qu?bec government to ensure the quality and safety of buildings and systems, including safety programs within the field of pressure vessels. Kotb has also been recently elected as president of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) for a oneyear term, which began in July 2013. Kotb is the 132nd president of ASME and the fourth woman to lead the engineering organization. She is a recipient of the ASME Dedicated Service Award and the Canadian Standards Association Award of Merit for her contribution to the development of Canadian nuclear standards.

articleTitle: A Builder and Teacher: Danowski Espouses the Benefits of Communities
abstract: Meredith Danowski was interested in engineering before she even knew exactly what engineering was. Growing up, her favorite toys were LEGOs and toy cars, and she loved to watch her grandfather at his workbench fixing things and putting new things together. In grade school, she realized she had a serious love for space and decided she wanted to be an astronaut. She hasn't looked back since.

articleTitle: Statistics Versus Personal Experience: Stories of IBM Technical Working Women Around the World [The Good, the Bad, & the Ugly: Engineering FACTS]
abstract: For most women who enter the fields of science and engineering, the road is often circuitous, with detours along the way. The stories that accompany these career paths are not only interesting but provide guidance and insight to those who read them, who are perhaps searching for their own way forward. The goal of this article is to bring forward and illuminate the success stories of a diverse set of IBM technical women from around the world, demonstrating the rich and varied ways they have worked cross-culturally and globally to achieve professional success.

articleTitle: Correction [to "Exit is the way in: All-girls competitive team excels in robotics"]
abstract: The "Exit Is the Way In" article that appeared in the June 2013 issue of IEEE Women in Engineering Magazine was incorrectly attributed to Katianne Williams. Leslie Prives was the author of the article. We apologize for the error.

articleTitle: Putting the "You" in Unique [Letter from the Editor]
abstract: Reflecting upon all of the talented people IEEE Women in Engineering Magazine has interviewed, it has become evident that the most successful individuals are those who have unique perspectives, which have led to major innovations that have impacted humanity. In other words, it is time to embrace what is unique and different about you. These are the qualities that foster diversity and innovation.

abstract: Provides a listing of current staff, committee members and society officers.

articleTitle: Situation Critical: Critical Theory and Critical Thinking in Engineering Education [Career Advisor]
abstract: In the last decade there has been an increased emphasis in engineering education on the development of critical thinking skills, owing in part to the introduction of the ABET 2000 criteria. Critical thinking in engineering education occurs mostly in a focused context, directed toward fulfilling one of several ABET learning outcomes. Reviewing the literature, one finds discussions of critical thinking in the contexts of problem solving [1]?[3], conducting experiments [4], [5], ethical decision-making [6], [7], open-ended design [8], [9], and assessing the social impacts of technology [10]. In this work, critical thinking is applied within these focused elements of engineering but not about engineering itself.

articleTitle: Tackling the Tech Gap: Chang Helping Women Access Technology [Women to Watch]
abstract: Ann Mei Chang, senior advisor for women and technology in the Secretary's Office of Global Women's Issues at the U.S. Department of State, serving as a Franklin fellow, has a big task on her hands. Her main focus is working on ways that technology can be leveraged to improve the lives of women and girls, particularly in the developing world. This includes three major areas: bridging the gender gap in access to technology, particularly mobile phones and the Internet in developing countries; finding effective ways to leverage technology solutions as a tool for social good and development, such as in health, education, agriculture, government, and entrepreneurship; and job and career opportunities for women in the technology sector.

articleTitle: New Year, New Objectives: Focusing on Four Main Goals in 2013 [Amperes: Current Affairs from Around the World]
A Creative and Innovative Problem Solver: Tabatabai Actively Involved in Recruitment and Mentoring [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Shirin Tabatabai was not sure she wanted to be an engineer until a conversation with a high school teacher sparked an idea. Her calculus teacher suggested either becoming a math teacher (which was immediately not appealing to her) or pursuing a career in engineering. She asked what engineers do and he stated, "they use creative, innovative ideas to solve problems." That immediately stoked her curiosity and after studying the field in her early college career, she pursued her electrical engineering degree. With assistance from Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E), she also completed her master's in power engineering. She has been with the utility company for ten years.

articleTitle: Shifting into High Gear: F1 in Schools Program Fosters STEM Interest [Pipelining: Attractive Programs for Women]
abstract: Georgia high schoolers Anna Awald, Kelly Fitzgerald, Claire McCoy, and Sabine Saldanha are taking off--fast! In the past two years, they have blown away their competition at various challenges, traveled the globe, and built a race car that won them the honor of fourth fastest car in the world, all thanks to the F1 in Schools program.

articleTitle: Segregation Connection: Engineering Bond Created Between Two Campuses [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: A love of engineering can be unifying; in fact, it is a common interest shared among the thousands of you reading this article across the globe right now. At the Ajman University of Science and Technology (AUST), engineering is the foundation for a bond shared across two segregated campuses, helping bring together the male and female students of a school where the opposite genders might only see each other once every few weeks.

articleTitle: Exit Is the Way In: All-Girls Competitive Team Excels in Robotics [Pipelining: Attractive Programs for Women]
abstract: It is often said that to develop talent and cultivate passion in people, we should "start them young." This is the premise under which extracurricular activities, such as sports, or cultural pursuits, like language or music, become so important in elementary and middle schools. It is also a key factor in supporting future generations of engineers, who need to recognize their aptitudes for science and math at an early age. It is why William Lam, a member of IEEE Women in Engineering (WIE), is volunteering his time to coach an all-girls competitive team in a robotics club.

articleTitle: No Limits: Davis Melds Knowledge of Technology and Law [Women to Watch]
abstract: Many people considering a future in engineering often pause at the college level, concerned that their future career options may somehow be limited if they pursue a ?narrow? degree path instead of liberal arts. Clara Davis, with a Ph.D. in engineering, a J.D., and a resume filled with time in engineering, law, and academia, is living proof that with the right attitude, there are no limits to where your engineering background can take you.

articleTitle: Ahead of Her Time: Savitz Bridges Two Worlds [Women to Watch]
abstract: Growing up in Philadelphia, Enid Jacobson Savitz often worked alongside her parents in the family candy store. It was the 1940s, and the Jacobson family lived above their mom-and-pop store with an assortment of other relatives in what Savitz's son Eric affectionately calls a "crazy, communal living arrangement."

articleTitle: Newton's Three Laws: Relating Patel's Corollaries [Amperes: Current Affairs from Around the World]
Achieving Career Gold: Lindner Offers Advice to Engineers [Career Advisor]
abstract: When it comes to achieving what Ken Lindner calls "career gold," the ball, as they say, is in your court, but not in the way you may think. It's not just the rare, clutch decisions that matter. Reaching professional success is about making the right decisions, large and small, day in and day out, so that you are consistently forging a career path that is in true alignment with your goals.

articleTitle: Resilience, strength, and triumph [Letter from the Editor]
abstract: Presents letters sent to the editor regarding previous articles from this publication or other relevant topics of discussion.

articleTitle: A Broad Perspective: Patent Law Suits Gordon Well [Women to Watch]
abstract: While working in network security for the telecommunications industry, Lori Gordon says she felt like she was in a "good versus evil" situation. "We would try to figure out how hackers would break the network next, so we could fix it before they did," she says. A few years later, Gordon parlayed that experience with technology and an attitude to defend into a successful career as a patent attorney, a transition she calls "the best career decision I could have ever made."

articleTitle: It's in Her Blood: Wright Using the Media to Empower Women [Amperes: Current Affairs from Around the World]
abstract: If you've seen True Blood, you?ve seen Tanya Wright. But these days, she's popping up in a lot of other places too, like the Clinton Global Initiative, one of the many avenues where she is using her media influence to bring attention to causes close to her heart.

articleTitle: The Next Wave of Innovation: Martinich Masters the Art of Science and Public Policy [Amperes: Current Affairs from Around the World]
abstract: Leslie Martinich is constantly looking to catch the next wave of innovation: she?s worked for a variety of start-ups, started her own management consulting firm that guides companies in leading innovation, and spent 2012 serving as the sole IEEE Congressional Fellow in Washington, D.C. In fact, Martinich began innovating at a young age when she acted against the expected societal norms and the advice she was given by teachers not to pursue her passions. ?When I was in high school, I really loved biology,? says Martinich. ?I told my teacher that I?d like to be a scientist, but she told me that there was no need, because all the world?s problems had already been solved by scientists.? Another teacher, after giving Martinich?s science group a company tour, told the students that they could ?have any job they want,? before quietly telling Leslie, the only female in the group, that she could be a librarian.

articleTitle: Information and Communication Tech in Serbia: Girls in ICT Day Encourages Young Women [Amperes: Current Affairs from Around the World]
abstract: Bojana Lecic grew up in a town in Serbia with her three sisters. She discovered her interest in the technical sciences during high school and decided to major in information technology (IT) at the University of Belgrade, where she is now in her senior year. Not many girls in Serbia decide to study IT, she says, because of the "predominant attitude that programmers are almost exclusively men. In the last couple of years, circumstances changed a little bit; however, [the] IT sector still remains mostly reserved for men."

articleTitle: Ethical Honor: Panetta wins Distinguished Ethical Practices Award [Amperes: Current Affairs from Around the World]
abstract: "For exemplary contributions and leadership in developing ethics and social responsibility in students," Dr. Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow, was named the 2013 IEEE Dinstinguished Ethical Practices Award winner. Dr. Panetta is a professor of electrical and computer Engineering at Tufts University and director of the Simulation Research Laboratory. Her research focuses on developing efficient algorithms for simulation, modeling, and signal and image processing for security and biomedical applications. A brief professional biography is given. She is the 2013 IEEE USA vice president of communications and the Editor-in-Chief of IEEE Women in Engineering Magazine.

articleTitle: Abou-Chadi Honored as 2013 Clementina Saduwa Award Winner : Egyptian Is a Pioneer in Biomedical Signal Processing [Amperes: Current Affairs from Around the World]
abstract: Prof. Fatma Abou-Chadi from Mansoura University in Egypt is the winner of the 2013 Clementina Saduwa award. Abou-Chadi received the recognition for her groundbreaking work in biomedical signal processing in Egypt and for her efforts to get more Egyptian women into biomedical engineering research. Abou-Chadi was the first Egyptian female engineer to earn a Ph.D. degree from Imperial College, London, in the field of biomedical signal processing, and she established the first research team in an Egyptian university led by a woman in biomedical signal processing. She was the first female engineering faculty member to become the dean of computers and information sciences at Mansoura University. Additionally, Abou-Chadi established a new bachelor?s of science degree at Mansoura University, the communications and information engineering program.

articleTitle: Helping Women Access Master-Level Training: Al-Wehaibi Awarded a Scholarship [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: IEEE Women in Engineering (WIE) is pleased to congratulate Buthayna Al- Wehaibi, who has been awarded a scholarship from the IE Business School in partnership with IEEE WIE. The IE Business School is a leading European institution of higher education, where Al-Wehaibi began studying for her M.B.A. earlier this year. IE and WIE are working together to help top women engineers access master?s- level training and build a professional network that will allow WIE members to advance their careers.

articleTitle: In Memoriam: Maria Batool: Bringing WIE to the Forefront [Amperes: Current Affairs from Around the World]
abstract: Recounts the life and  professional achievements of Maria Batool.
